popes.name: Pope Clement I
popes.cat: Early Church · Saint
popes.bio: One of the first popes to lead the Church of Rome straight after the apostles. Tradition says he knew Peter and learned from him.
secs: His life
Very little is known about his life. Early sources remember him as a leading elder of the Roman community who had known Peter and Paul. Tradition says he died a martyr.
The letter to the Corinthians

His letter to the Church in Corinth, written around the year 96, is one of the oldest Christian texts outside the New Testament. When the leaders of the Corinthian community were unjustly removed, this letter from Rome called them back to peace and order. It shows the Church of Rome already caring for the troubles of other churches in those early years.
docs: A call to peace and order; one of the oldest Christian letters outside the New Testament.

popes.name: Pope Callixtus I
popes.cat: A former slave who became pope, and a martyr · Saint
popes.bio: In his youth he was a slave; he served a sentence in the mines and later came to lead the Church of Rome. The catacomb that bears his name is one of the most visited in Rome today.
secs: From slave to pope

While a slave of a Christian master he lost money in a banking venture and was sent to the mines of Sardinia. Once freed, Pope Zephyrinus put him in charge of the Christian cemetery on the Via Appia, known today as the Catacomb of St. Callixtus.
A pope of mercy
He held that great sinners who repented should be welcomed back into the Church. This brought him into a deep dispute with Hippolytus, who took a hard line. He was martyred around 222.

popes.name: Pope Sylvester I
popes.cat: Pope of the Council of Nicaea · Saint
popes.bio: He became pope just after the Edict of Milan gave Christians their freedom. The first ecumenical council met in his time, at Nicaea (İznik) in 325.
secs: The first years of freedom

After three centuries of persecution, under Emperor Constantine the Church could at last live openly. During Sylvester’s papacy the Lateran Basilica and the first basilica over the tomb of St. Peter were built in Rome.
His link to Turkey

Because of his age he could not go himself to the first ecumenical council, held at Nicaea (İznik) in 325; he sent two priests to represent him. The council declared that Christ is of the same substance as the Father and laid the foundation of the Creed still said today.

popes.name: Pope Damasus I
popes.cat: Pope of the Vulgate · Saint
popes.bio: He asked his secretary, St. Jerome, to make a new Latin translation of the Bible. Known as the Vulgate, it was the Western Church’s Bible for more than a thousand years.
secs: With Jerome

Damasus was troubled by the differences between the old Latin translations of the Bible. Around 382 he asked Jerome to revise the Gospels; in the years that followed Jerome translated the whole Bible.
The tombs of the martyrs
He restored the martyrs’ tombs in the catacombs of Rome and had poems in their honour carved in marble; some of these inscriptions are still in place today.

popes.name: Pope Celestine I
popes.cat: Pope of the Council of Ephesus · Saint
popes.bio: The Council of Ephesus, which honoured Mary as the “Mother of God”, met in his time. He also sent Ireland its first bishop.
secs: His link to Turkey

He sent his legates to the council held at Ephesus in 431. The council declared that it is right to call Mary “Theotokos”, Mother of God. The ruins of the Church of Mary, where the council met, can still be seen at Ephesus.
Ireland
In 431 he sent Palladius as bishop to the Christians of Ireland. Tradition says St. Patrick went to the island soon afterwards to carry on this mission.

popes.name: Pope Leo I (the Great)
popes.cat: Doctor of the Church · Saint
popes.bio: The first pope to be called “the Great”. His letter explaining that Jesus is true God and true man was read out at the Council of Chalcedon.
secs: The Tome of Leo

In 449 he wrote to Flavian, Patriarch of Constantinople, explaining clearly that Christ has two natures, divine and human, in one person. When the letter was read at the council held at Chalcedon (Kadıköy) in 451, the bishops are said to have cried out: “Peter has spoken through Leo.”
Meeting Attila

When Attila the Hun invaded Italy in 452, Leo led the delegation that went out to meet him. Attila withdrew and Rome was spared. Three years later, when the Vandals sacked the city, Leo tried to talk them out of burning and slaughter.
His link to Turkey
The Council of Chalcedon, which accepted Leo’s teaching, met in what is now the Kadıköy district of Istanbul. It gave the basic statement of faith about Christ that is still used today.
docs: Two natures in Christ, one person. Read at the Council of Chalcedon.
About a hundred sermons on Christmas, Easter and fasting.

popes.name: Pope Hormisdas
popes.cat: Pope of peace with the East · Saint
popes.bio: He ended a thirty-five-year split between Rome and Constantinople with the statement of faith that bears his name.
secs: The Acacian schism
In 484 the bond between the Churches of Rome and Constantinople was broken. Hormisdas patiently worked to heal the rift, sending envoys to the East.
His link to Turkey

In 519 Patriarch John II of Constantinople and Emperor Justin I signed the “Formula of Hormisdas”. It acknowledged that the Catholic faith had always been kept spotless in the Church of Rome. With it, Constantinople and Rome were reunited.
docs: A statement of faith signed by the Eastern bishops, expressing their loyalty to the see of Peter.

popes.name: Pope Gregory I (the Great)
popes.cat: Doctor of the Church · Saint
popes.bio: While prefect of Rome he gave up everything to become a monk. As pope he called himself “the servant of the servants of God”, a title popes still use.
secs: His life

He came from a wealthy Roman family and became prefect of the city as a young man. When his father died he used his inheritance to found monasteries and became a monk himself. He was elected pope in years of plague and famine; he fed the poor and in practice governed the city.
A mission to England
In 596 he sent the monk Augustine (Augustine of Canterbury) with a few companions to England. Through this mission Christianity spread among the Anglo-Saxons.
His link to Turkey
Before becoming pope he lived in Constantinople for about six years as Rome’s envoy. There he came to know the Eastern Church and the imperial court at close hand.
docs: How a shepherd of souls should live and teach; for centuries the handbook of bishops.
The lives of Italian saints, above all St. Benedict.

popes.name: Pope Martin I
popes.cat: Martyr pope tried in Constantinople · Saint
popes.bio: He defended the two wills of Christ against the emperor; he was arrested, tried in Constantinople and died in exile. He is the last pope honoured as a martyr.
secs: The Lateran Synod
At the synod he called in Rome in 649 he openly declared that Christ has both a divine and a human will, despite Emperor Constans II’s decree forbidding the debate.
His link to Turkey

In 653 the emperor’s soldiers arrested him in Rome and brought him to Constantinople. He was tried while ill, paraded through the streets in chains and exiled to Cherson in the Crimea. He died there in 655; his letters speak of hunger and loneliness.

popes.name: Pope Agatho
popes.cat: Pope of the Third Council of Constantinople · Saint
popes.bio: His letter explaining that Christ has both a divine and a human will was read with joy at the council held in Constantinople.
secs: Two wills
At the time some taught that Christ had only one will. Agatho explained that because Christ is true God and true man he has two wills, and that his human will freely submits to the divine will.
His link to Turkey
When his letter was read at the Sixth Ecumenical Council in Constantinople in 680-681, the council fathers cried out: “Peter has spoken through Agatho.”
docs: The doctrinal letter, read at the council, explaining the two wills in Christ.

popes.name: Pope Sergius I
popes.cat: Son of a family from Antioch · Saint
popes.bio: He was the son of a Syrian family that had moved from Antioch to Sicily. He added to the Mass the “Lamb of God” (Agnus Dei) that is sung at every Mass today.
secs: The Lamb of God
He added to the Roman Mass the prayer “Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world”, sung at the breaking of the bread. He also began the processions held on the feasts of Mary.
His link to Turkey

In 692 he refused to sign some of the decisions of the Quinisext (Trullan) Synod in Constantinople. Emperor Justinian II sent an officer to arrest him; but the people and soldiers of Rome and Ravenna protected the pope, and the officer saved his life by hiding under the pope’s bed.

popes.name: Pope Zachary
popes.cat: A pope of Greek origin · Saint
popes.bio: He was among the last popes of Greek origin. His peaceful diplomacy protected Rome from Lombard attacks.
secs: An envoy of peace
He went in person to meet the Lombard king Liutprand and, without a battle, won back the cities that had been seized.
Between two worlds
He translated Pope Gregory I’s “Dialogues” into Greek for the Christians of the East. In the West, the bond he formed with the Frankish king Pepin shaped the centuries that followed in Europe.

popes.name: Pope Adrian I
popes.cat: Pope of the Second Council of Nicaea
popes.bio: His twenty-three-year papacy is one of the longest since Peter. The Council of Nicaea that restored the veneration of holy icons met in his time.
secs: His link to Turkey

He sent his legates to the Seventh Ecumenical Council, held at Nicaea (İznik) in 787. The council put an end to the destruction of icons and taught that honour shown to an image passes to the person it depicts.
Charlemagne
He was a close friend of the Frankish king Charlemagne. Grieved by his death, Charlemagne had a marble epitaph made for Adrian; it is in St. Peter’s Basilica today.

popes.name: Pope Leo III
popes.cat: The pope who crowned Charlemagne · Saint
popes.bio: On Christmas night in the year 800, in St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome, he crowned Charlemagne emperor.
secs: Christmas 800

After he was attacked in Rome he took refuge with the Frankish king Charlemagne. On 25 December 800 he crowned Charlemagne “Emperor of the Romans”. This is seen as the beginning of the idea of the Holy Roman Empire, which would last for centuries in the West.

popes.name: Pope Nicholas I
popes.cat: Nicholas “the Great” · Saint
popes.bio: He defended the indissolubility of marriage against kings, and guided a whole people into Christianity with his long replies to the Bulgarians.
secs: Replies to the Bulgarians

In 866 the Bulgarian king Boris sent more than a hundred questions for his newly Christian people. Nicholas’s answers are full of gentle, practical advice on baptism, fasting, marriage and justice. In the same letter he writes that extracting confessions by torture is forbidden.
His link to Turkey
He opposed the unjust removal of Ignatius, Patriarch of Constantinople. This dispute was one of the first steps in the long tensions between Rome and Constantinople.
docs: 106 answers to the questions of the Bulgarians.

popes.name: Pope Formosus
popes.cat: Missionary to Bulgaria · the “Cadaver Synod”
popes.bio: As a young man he was a missionary who preached the Gospel to the Bulgarians. After his death his body was dug up and put on trial; the event, known as the “Cadaver Synod”, stands for one of the darkest times in the Church’s history.
secs: In Bulgaria
In 866 Pope Nicholas I sent him as bishop to the newly Christian Bulgarians. King Boris loved him so much that he wanted him to become archbishop of Bulgaria.
The Cadaver Synod

In 897 his successor Stephen VI, out of political spite, had Formosus’s body taken from the grave, dressed in papal vestments, seated on a throne and put on trial. The people were outraged by the scandal; Stephen was deposed that same year. Later popes restored Formosus’s good name.

popes.name: Pope Sylvester II
popes.cat: The scholar pope · the pope of the year 1000
popes.bio: He was a mathematician, astronomer and teacher. He was one of those who brought Arabic numerals and the abacus to Western Europe, and he entered the year 1000 as pope.
secs: Gerbert

His real name was Gerbert. As a young man he studied mathematics and astronomy in Spain, in monasteries where the learning of al-Andalus flowed in. At his school in Reims he used celestial spheres and the abacus in his lessons.
The first French pope
Elected in 999, he was the first French pope. By setting up the Church structures of Hungary and Poland, he helped bring Central Europe into the Christian world.

popes.name: Pope Leo IX
popes.cat: A reforming pope · Saint
popes.bio: He travelled the length of Europe to free the Church from bribery and worldliness. The end of his papacy was overshadowed by the split between East and West in 1054.
secs: A pope on the road
He spent most of his five-year papacy travelling, holding synods in Italy, France and Germany. He began a determined fight against the buying and selling of Church offices.
His link to Turkey

In 1054 he sent envoys to Constantinople. After Leo died in April, on 16 July 1054 Cardinal Humbert laid the bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia. The event became the symbol of the split between East and West; the mutual excommunications were lifted in 1965 by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras.

popes.name: Pope Gregory VII
popes.cat: The reforming pope · Saint
popes.bio: He fought to make the Church independent of kings and money. Emperor Henry IV waited in the snow at Canossa for his forgiveness.
secs: The Gregorian reform
In his day Church offices were often sold for money and bishops were appointed by kings. Gregory opposed this and firmly upheld the celibate life of priests.
Canossa

He clashed with Emperor Henry IV over the right to appoint bishops, and cut him off from the Church. In the winter of 1077 the emperor waited for three days as a penitent outside the castle of Canossa in northern Italy, and was forgiven.
Death in exile
The conflict later flared up again. Gregory had to leave Rome and died in Salerno. His last words are said to have been: “I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.”
docs: 27 short statements on the authority of the pope.

popes.name: Pope Urban II
popes.cat: Blessed
popes.bio: His speech at Clermont in 1095 launched the First Crusade.
secs: Clermont

The Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos asked the West for help against the Seljuk advance in Anatolia. In 1095 at Clermont, Urban called on Western Christians to help the Christians of the East and to go to Jerusalem.
His link to Turkey

The crusaders besieged Nicaea (İznik) in 1097 and crossed Anatolia to reach Antioch. The crusades left deep marks on the lands of today’s Turkey; today the Church also openly acknowledges the dark sides of that time.

popes.name: Pope Adrian IV
popes.cat: The only English pope
popes.bio: Born Nicholas Breakspear, he is the only Englishman ever to have been pope. He entered a monastery in France as an ordinary monk, became its abbot, and rose from there to the papacy.
secs: In Scandinavia
Before becoming pope he went to Norway and Sweden as papal legate; in 1152 he founded the first archdiocese of the Church in Norway.
With the emperor
In 1155 he crowned Frederick Barbarossa emperor; but a long power struggle between pope and emperor soon began.

popes.name: Pope Innocent III
popes.cat: The most powerful pope of the Middle Ages
popes.bio: He became pope at 37. He approved the little brotherhood of St. Francis and called one of the most important councils of the Middle Ages.
secs: Meeting Francis
In 1209 he received Francis of Assisi and his companions, who had come to Rome in poor clothes, and gave spoken approval to their rule of life. So the Franciscan Order was born.
The Fourth Lateran Council

The council he called in 1215 made it a rule that every Catholic go to confession at least once a year and receive Communion at Easter. The term “transubstantiation” for the change in the Eucharist was also used officially at this council.
His link to Turkey

The Fourth Crusade, launched at his call, turned on Constantinople in 1204 and the city was sacked. Innocent condemned the attack in strong words; the sack deepened the wound between the Eastern and Western Churches.
docs: Decrees of the Fourth Lateran Council
The rule of yearly confession and Easter Communion.

popes.name: Pope Gregory X
popes.cat: Founder of the conclave · Blessed
popes.bio: The longest election in the Church’s history ended, after almost three years, with his name. When the news reached him he was a pilgrim in Acre and not yet even a priest.
secs: Behind closed doors

So that such a long wait would never happen again, in 1274 he made it a rule that the cardinals elect the pope shut away from the outside world. The “conclave” (a room locked with a key) still rests on this rule.
The Second Council of Lyon

At the council he called in 1274, the envoys of the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII accepted union with Rome. The union did not last, but Gregory’s greatest hope was to bring East and West together again.
docs: The constitution requiring the pope to be elected in a closed conclave.

popes.name: Pope John XXI
popes.cat: The physician pope · the only Portuguese pope
popes.bio: He was a famous physician and logician; his medical book was read for centuries. In the eighth month of his papacy the ceiling of his study collapsed on him.
secs: Peter of Spain
He is known as Petrus Hispanus. His textbook on logic was taught in universities for centuries, and his medical book, “The Treasury of the Poor”, gave practical remedies for ordinary people.
In Viterbo
He had an extra room built for study in his palace at Viterbo. In May 1277 its ceiling fell in, and he died a few days later.
docs: The standard logic textbook of the medieval universities.

popes.name: Pope Celestine V
popes.cat: The hermit who stepped down · Saint
popes.bio: He was an eighty-year-old hermit living in the mountains; he was elected pope and, five months later, seeing that he could not carry the burden, he resigned.
secs: Pietro da Morrone
From his youth he lived a life of prayer and fasting in the mountains of Abruzzo; with the monks who gathered around him he founded a community later known as the Celestines.
A humble farewell
On 13 December 1294 he freely renounced the papacy. In 2009 Pope Benedict XVI visited his tomb in L’Aquila and left his own pallium on it; four years later he too stepped down.

popes.name: Pope Boniface VIII
popes.cat: The first Jubilee Year
popes.bio: In 1300 he proclaimed the first Holy Year (Jubilee) in the Church’s history. He clashed fiercely with King Philip IV of France.
secs: The first Jubilee
In 1300 he offered a special pardon to pilgrims who came to Rome. The tradition of the Holy Year has continued ever since; the last ordinary Jubilee was celebrated in 2025.
Anagni
He issued the bull Unam Sanctam against the power of kings over the Church. In 1303 the king’s men seized him in his home town of Anagni; he died soon afterwards.
docs: On the unity and spiritual authority of the Church.

popes.name: Pope Martin V
popes.cat: The pope who ended the schism
popes.bio: The Great Western Schism, when two and then three men claimed to be pope at the same time, ended with his election.
secs: Constance

Since 1378 the Western Church had had more than one claimant to the papacy, and Europe was split in two, then in three. The Council of Constance persuaded the rivals to withdraw and elected Martin in 1417.
Back to Rome
After many years he settled the papacy in Rome again and began to repair the ruined city.

popes.name: Pope Eugene IV
popes.cat: Pope of the Council of Florence
popes.bio: He sat down in Florence with the Byzantine emperor and the Patriarch of Constantinople; in 1439 the union of East and West was proclaimed.
secs: His link to Turkey

Emperor John VIII Palaiologos and Patriarch Joseph II came from Constantinople to Italy with hundreds of Greek clergy. The union was proclaimed on 6 July 1439 with the decree “Laetentur Caeli” (Let the heavens rejoice).
Armenians and Syriacs

In 1439 the same council signed a decree of union with the Armenian Church, and in the following years with the Copts and the Syriacs. The history of the Armenian and Syriac Catholic communities in Turkey is linked to these efforts too.
docs: The council’s decree proclaiming union with the Greek Church.
The decree of union with the Armenians; an explanation of the seven sacraments.

popes.name: Pope Nicholas V
popes.cat: Founder of the Vatican Library
popes.bio: He was a scholar who loved books. With the hundreds of manuscripts he collected he laid the foundation of the Vatican Library. The fall of Constantinople happened in his time.
secs: Books
He paid scholars to translate Greek works into Latin; when he died the library held more than a thousand manuscripts.
His link to Turkey
Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453. Nicholas helped to save the books carried by Greek scholars fleeing the city; some of these manuscripts are still in the Vatican Library today.

popes.name: Pope Callixtus III
popes.cat: The pope of the noon bell
popes.bio: The custom of ringing church bells at noon goes back to a call he made. He had the trial of Joan of Arc reopened and cleared her name.
secs: The noon bell

During the siege of Belgrade in 1456 he asked all Christians to pray together at noon when the bell rang. With the news from Belgrade this bell became a call to prayer at noon; together with the Angelus it continues today.
Joan of Arc
He ordered a new hearing of the case of Joan of Arc, who had been burned in 1431; in 1456 the court declared her innocent. Joan was declared a saint in 1920.

popes.name: Pope Pius II
popes.cat: The writer pope · a letter to Mehmed the Conqueror
popes.bio: He was one of the famous writers of the Renaissance and the only pope to tell his own life story. He wrote a long letter addressed to Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror.
secs: Enea Silvio

As a young man he wrote poems and a love story, and travelled Europe as a diplomat. As pope he wrote his memoirs, the “Commentarii”. He had the village where he was born rebuilt and named it Pienza; today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site as a Renaissance town.
His link to Turkey

In 1461 he wrote a long letter to Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror inviting him to become a Christian; no one knows whether it was ever sent. He died in Ancona in 1464, waiting for a fleet that never came.
docs: The only autobiography written by a pope.

popes.name: Pope Sixtus IV
popes.cat: Pope of the Sistine Chapel
popes.bio: He was a Franciscan theologian. The Sistine Chapel, where popes are elected today, bears his name.
secs: The Sistine Chapel

The walls of the chapel he built between 1477 and 1481 were painted by artists such as Botticelli, Perugino and Ghirlandaio. The ceiling and the Last Judgement were painted by Michelangelo years later.
A library for all
In 1475 he opened the Vatican Library to scholars and appointed its first librarian. He also approved the feast of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin with its own liturgical texts.

popes.name: Pope Julius II
popes.cat: The pope of art
popes.bio: He laid the foundation stone of the new St. Peter’s Basilica, had Michelangelo paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, and founded the Swiss Guard.
secs: Art
In 1506 he laid the foundation stone of today’s St. Peter’s Basilica. Between 1508 and 1512 he had Michelangelo paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and Raphael paint the rooms of the Vatican.
The Swiss Guard
The Swiss Guard he founded in 1506 still protects the pope and is one of the oldest military units in active service in the world.

popes.name: Pope Leo X
popes.cat: The Renaissance pope
popes.bio: A Medici, he was a pope who loved art and Raphael. Luther’s Reformation began in his time.
secs: Art and debt
While money was being raised to rebuild St. Peter’s Basilica, the abuse of indulgences caused controversy. That controversy sparked Luther’s 95 theses in 1517.
Luther

In 1520, with “Exsurge Domine”, he condemned forty-one of Luther’s propositions; when Luther did not back down he was excommunicated in 1521. The deep reform of the Church would be the work of later popes and of the Council of Trent.

popes.name: Pope Paul III
popes.cat: The pope who opened Trent
popes.bio: He approved the Jesuit Order and called the Council of Trent, the most important council of the Catholic Reformation.
secs: The Jesuits
In 1540 he formally approved the Society of Jesus (the Jesuits), founded by Ignatius of Loyola and his companions.
The Council of Trent
After the Protestant Reformation he called the Council of Trent in 1545. The council set out the Catholic faith clearly and renewed the Church deeply, from the training of priests to the liturgy.
The Last Judgement
He had Michelangelo paint the Last Judgement on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel.
docs: The approval of the Jesuit Order.

popes.name: Pope Pius IV
popes.cat: The pope who completed the Council of Trent
popes.bio: He reopened the Council of Trent, which had been suspended for ten years, and brought it to a successful close in 1563.
secs: Trent

The council set out clearly the Catholic teaching on Scripture and Tradition, the sacraments and justification, and called for seminaries to train candidates for the priesthood. Pius confirmed its decrees in 1564.
St. Charles Borromeo
He brought his nephew Charles Borromeo to work beside him. Charles became a great bishop who put the council’s decrees into practice, and a saint.
docs: The profession of faith used after the Council of Trent.

popes.name: Pope Pius V
popes.cat: The rosary pope · Saint
popes.bio: He was a Dominican friar and kept wearing the white Dominican habit as pope; the popes’ custom of wearing white is said to come from him. He credited the victory at Lepanto to the rosary.
secs: Putting Trent into practice

He put the decrees of the Council of Trent into effect: the Roman Catechism (1566), the revised Breviary (1568) and the Roman Missal of 1570 were published in his time. That Missal was used for almost four hundred years.
Lepanto and the rosary

In 1571 he formed a Holy League against the Ottoman fleet and called all Christians to pray the rosary. After the victory at Lepanto on 7 October 1571 he declared that day the feast of “Our Lady of Victory”; today it is celebrated as the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary.
His link to Turkey
The Battle of Lepanto was the Ottoman Empire’s first great defeat at sea. The Catholic world credited the victory to the rosary; the story of the battle is told on the History of the Rosary page.
docs: Set the rosary in its present form.
Promulgated the Roman Missal for the whole Latin Church.

popes.name: Pope Gregory XIII
popes.cat: The pope of the calendar
popes.bio: The calendar used by almost the whole world today bears his name: the Gregorian calendar.
secs: Calendar reform

Over the centuries the Julian calendar had fallen about ten days behind the true solar year, and the date of Easter was drifting. The new calendar Gregory had scientists prepare came into force in 1582: the day after Thursday 4 October was Friday 15 October.
Education
He enlarged the Jesuit college in Rome; today, as the Pontifical Gregorian University, it bears his name.
His link to Turkey
Turkey adopted the Gregorian calendar on 1 January 1926. The dates we use today rest on the calculations made in his time.
docs: The papal bull that brought in the Gregorian calendar.

popes.name: Pope Sixtus V
popes.cat: The pope who rebuilt Rome
popes.bio: A shepherd boy who became a Franciscan. In five years he reshaped Rome’s streets, aqueducts and squares; the dome of St. Peter’s was completed in his time.
secs: The dome and the obelisk
In 1586 he had the obelisk brought from Egypt raised in the middle of St. Peter’s Square. In 1590 the dome designed by Michelangelo was completed by Giacomo della Porta.
Cardinals and congregations
He limited the number of cardinals to seventy and divided the government of the Vatican into fifteen congregations. This arrangement was used for centuries.
docs: The constitution that divided the Roman Curia into congregations.

popes.name: Pope Urban VIII
popes.cat: Bernini’s pope · the pope of the Galileo affair
popes.bio: A portrait of him as a young man is attributed to Caravaggio; as pope he commissioned Bernini’s magnificent baldachin in St. Peter’s Basilica. The Galileo affair took place in his time.
secs: A pope of the arts
Maffeo Barberini consecrated the new St. Peter’s Basilica in 1626. Bernini’s bronze baldachin and the Palazzo Barberini are works of his time.
Galileo

At first he was a friend of Galileo; but after his “Dialogue” was published in 1632, Galileo was tried in 1633 and sentenced to house arrest. In 1992, in a speech by John Paul II, the Church acknowledged the errors made in the case.

popes.name: Pope Innocent XI
popes.cat: The pope of simple living · Blessed
popes.bio: He lived very simply himself and cut back extravagance in the Vatican. The siege of Vienna in 1683 happened during his papacy.
secs: Simplicity
He ended the habit of handing out offices and wealth to relatives and reduced the debts of the Papal States. He was beatified in 1956.
Vienna 1683

When the Ottoman army besieged Vienna he backed the alliance between King Jan Sobieski of Poland and Emperor Leopold I and sent great help. The lifting of the siege is remembered as a turning point in European history.

popes.name: Pope Benedict XIV
popes.cat: The pope of the first encyclical
popes.bio: He was one of the most learned jurists of his day. Ubi Primum, issued in the first year of his papacy, is counted as the first encyclical in the modern sense.
secs: The path to sainthood
The great work he wrote before becoming pope set out in detail the steps for declaring someone blessed and a saint; its rules were used for a long time.
Science and friendship
He corresponded with scientists and supported the universities. He was respected even among Protestants.
docs: To the bishops on their duties; the first encyclical in the modern sense.

popes.name: Pope Clement XIV
popes.cat: The pope who suppressed the Jesuits
popes.bio: He was a Franciscan priest. Under pressure from the kings of Europe he suppressed the Jesuit Order in 1773; he founded the Pio-Clementine Museum in the Vatican.
secs: The Jesuits

The kings of Portugal, Spain and France wanted the Jesuits abolished. After long hesitation, in 1773 Clement suppressed the order with “Dominus ac Redemptor”. The order was restored in 1814 by Pius VII.
The museum
To display ancient statues he founded the Pio-Clementine Museum, the core of today’s Vatican Museums.
docs: The papal brief that suppressed the Jesuit Order.

popes.name: Pope Pius VII
popes.cat: Napoleon’s prisoner
popes.bio: He signed an agreement with Napoleon and attended his coronation, then spent five years as his prisoner.
secs: Napoleon
The Concordat he signed with France in 1801 allowed the Church to live openly in France again after the Revolution. In 1804 he was present in Paris at Napoleon’s coronation as emperor.
Captivity

When he opposed Napoleon’s annexation of the Papal States in 1809 he was arrested and held prisoner in Savona and Fontainebleau until 1814. Once free he returned to Rome, and that same year he restored the Jesuit Order.

popes.name: Pope Gregory XVI
popes.cat: The pope against the slave trade
popes.bio: He was a Camaldolese monk, and the last pope elected who was not yet a bishop. He openly condemned the slave trade.
secs: Slavery
With “In supremo apostolatus” in 1839 he expressly forbade Christians to enslave Africans and other peoples and to take part in the slave trade.
The missions
He founded new dioceses all over the world and encouraged the training of local clergy. In his time the missions in Asia, Africa and the Americas grew greatly.
docs: The apostolic letter condemning the slave trade.
An encyclical on the currents of thought of the time.

popes.name: Pope Pius IX
popes.cat: The longest papacy · Blessed
popes.bio: His papacy of more than 31 years is the longest that can be verified historically. He defined the Immaculate Conception as a truth of faith and called the First Vatican Council.
secs: The Immaculate Conception

In 1854 he defined as a truth of faith that Mary was preserved from original sin from the moment of her conception. Four years later Mary, appearing at Lourdes, introduced herself with the words “I am the Immaculate Conception”.
The First Vatican Council

The council held in 1869-1870 defined that the pope is infallible when he formally teaches on faith and morals. That same year the Papal States were absorbed into Italy, and Pius regarded himself as “the prisoner of the Vatican”.
Beatification
He was beatified by John Paul II in 2000.
docs: Warnings against the currents of thought of the time.
The First Vatican Council: the infallibility of the pope.

popes.name: Pope Leo XIII
popes.cat: The pope of workers and of the rosary
popes.bio: In the middle of the industrial revolution he wrote Rerum Novarum, defending the rights of workers; it is counted as the start of Catholic social teaching. He lived to the age of 93.
secs: Rerum Novarum

The encyclical he issued in 1891 defended workers’ rights to a fair wage, to rest and to form unions; it criticised both unbridled capitalism and the socialism that wanted to abolish private property.
The rosary pope
He wrote eleven encyclicals on the rosary and proposed October as the month of the rosary.
Back to St. Thomas
In the encyclical Aeterni Patris he put forward the philosophy of St. Thomas Aquinas as the foundation of Catholic schools.
His link to Leo XIV
Leo XIV, elected in 2025, said he chose his name in his memory: just as Leo XIII answered the industrial revolution, the Church today must answer the questions of the age of artificial intelligence.
docs: On the philosophy of St. Thomas Aquinas.
The first of his encyclicals on the rosary.
The rights of workers; the start of Catholic social teaching.
On the study of Holy Scripture.

popes.name: Pope Pius X
popes.cat: The pope of the Eucharist · Saint
popes.bio: He came from a poor village family and rose from village priest to pope. He allowed children to make their First Communion at an early age.
secs: Frequent Communion

Until then children usually made their First Communion at 12 to 14. In 1910 Pius X laid down that children could receive Communion once they reached the age of reason, about seven, and he encouraged the faithful to receive Communion often.
To restore all things in Christ
His motto as pope was “To restore all things in Christ”. He began the work of gathering the Church’s law into a single code; it was completed in 1917.
His death and canonisation
He died in the first days of the First World War, broken by the suffering of the war. He was declared a saint in 1954.
docs: Against the current of thought called Modernism.
First Communion for children at an early age.

popes.name: Pope Benedict XV
popes.cat: The pope of peace
popes.bio: He was elected at the start of the First World War and called the war “a senseless slaughter”. There is a statue of him in Istanbul, put up by the Turks.
secs: In the war years

In 1917 he put a concrete peace plan to the warring powers; it was not accepted. Through the Vatican he arranged for news to reach the families of prisoners of war and for wounded prisoners to be exchanged.
His link to Turkey

During the war he helped those who suffered, whatever their religion or nation. For this, in 1921, people of different faiths and nations in Istanbul paid for a statue of him in the garden of the Cathedral of the Holy Spirit in Harbiye. The inscription on its base honours him as “the benefactor of the peoples, without distinction of nationality or religion”.
Canon law
In 1917 he promulgated the first Code of Canon Law, begun by Pius X.
docs: The causes of the war and a call to peace.
The missions and the training of local priests.

popes.name: Pope Pius XI
popes.cat: Founder of Vatican City State
popes.bio: Vatican City State was founded in his time. He wrote outspoken encyclicals against both Nazism and communism.
secs: The Lateran Treaty
The treaty signed with Italy in 1929 founded Vatican City State and settled the “Roman Question” that had dragged on since 1870.
Christ the King
In 1925 he instituted the feast of Christ the King: however strong states and ideologies may seem, the last word belongs to Christ.
Against totalitarian regimes

In 1937 the encyclical Mit brennender Sorge (With burning concern), written in German, was smuggled into Germany and read out in every church; it criticised Nazi ideology. A few days later came the encyclical Divini Redemptoris against communism.
docs: The feast of Christ the King.
The social order, forty years after Rerum Novarum.

popes.name: Pope Pius XII
popes.cat: The pope of the Second World War years
popes.bio: He was elected just before the Second World War. He defined the Assumption of Mary as a truth of faith.
secs: The war years

His papacy fell in the darkest years of the war. During the war many Jews in Rome were hidden in Church institutions. The pope’s conduct during the war is still debated among historians; the Vatican archives were opened to researchers in 2020.
The Assumption of Mary
In 1950 he defined as a truth of faith that at the end of her earthly life Mary was taken up body and soul into heaven. The feast is kept every year on 15 August.
Biblical studies
The encyclical Divino Afflante Spiritu of 1943 encouraged Catholic scholars to study the Bible in its original languages and its historical setting.
docs: The Church, the Body of Christ.

popes.name: Pope John XXIII
popes.cat: “The pope who loved the Turks” · Saint
popes.bio: Before becoming pope he lived in Istanbul for ten years and learned Turkish. He is the pope who called the Second Vatican Council.
secs: The Istanbul years

From 1935 to 1944 Angelo Roncalli lived in Istanbul as the Vatican’s representative to Turkey and Greece. He learned Turkish and began having some prayers said in Turkish in the cathedral in Harbiye. He is known to have helped many Jews fleeing Europe during the Second World War. In Turkey he is remembered as “the pope who loved the Turks”; a street in Istanbul bears his name and there is a statue of him in the garden of the Basilica of St. Anthony.
The Second Vatican Council

He was elected at 77, expected to be a caretaker pope. But three months later, to the surprise of the whole world, he announced that he would call a council. The Second Vatican Council opened on 11 October 1962.
“The Good Pope”
He was loved for his warmth and humour; the Italians called him “the good pope”. In 2014 he was declared a saint on the same day as John Paul II.
docs: Peace on earth; the first encyclical addressed “to all men of good will”.

popes.name: Pope Paul VI
popes.cat: The pope who completed the Council · Saint
popes.bio: He brought the Second Vatican Council to a close. He was the first pope to fly to five continents; in 1967 he visited Istanbul and Ephesus.
secs: Completing the Council
In 1965 he closed the Second Vatican Council and began putting its decisions into practice.
Reconciliation with the Orthodox
In 1964 he embraced Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras in Jerusalem. On 7 December 1965 Rome and Constantinople lifted at the same moment the excommunications they had pronounced on each other in 1054.
His link to Turkey
In July 1967 he came to Turkey: in Istanbul he visited Athenagoras at the Ecumenical Patriarchate in Fener, then went to the House of the Virgin Mary near Ephesus and to İzmir.
Canonisation
He was declared a saint by Pope Francis in 2018.
docs: The development of peoples and justice.
Human life and the meaning of love in marriage.
Proclaiming the Gospel in our time.

popes.name: Pope John Paul I
popes.cat: The smiling pope · Blessed
popes.bio: His papacy lasted only 33 days. For his simple, warm manner he was called “the smiling pope”.
secs: 33 days
Albino Luciani was elected on 26 August 1978 and was the first pope to take the names of both his predecessors. He died in his sleep on 28 September 1978.
His style
He explained things simply, as if talking to children. He preferred to say “I” rather than the formal papal “we”, and he did without a coronation.
Beatification
He was beatified by Pope Francis in 2022.

popes.name: Pope Benedict XVI
popes.cat: The pope of faith and reason
popes.bio: Joseph Ratzinger, one of the leading theologians of the century. He became the first pope in about 600 years to step down of his own will.
secs: The theologian

At the Second Vatican Council he was a young adviser. For many years he headed the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith and led the preparation of the Catechism of the Catholic Church. As pope he wrote the three volumes of “Jesus of Nazareth”.
His link to Turkey
In November 2006 he visited Turkey: Ankara, the House of the Virgin Mary near Ephesus, and Istanbul. In Istanbul he visited the Sultan Ahmed Mosque.
Stepping down
In 2013, because of his age and strength, he stepped down. He lived in prayer in a monastery in the Vatican and died on 31 December 2022.
docs: Love in truth; the global economy and the human person.

popes.name: Pope Francis
popes.cat: The first pope from the Americas
popes.bio: The Argentine Jesuit Jorge Mario Bergoglio. He was the first pope to take the name of St. Francis of Assisi, and he put the poor and mercy at the centre.
secs: His life
He was born in Buenos Aires into a family of Italian immigrants. He became a Jesuit, and as archbishop of the city he was known as a bishop who took the bus and visited the slums.
Mercy
He declared 2015-2016 a Year of Mercy. Throughout his papacy he said the Church should turn to the wounded like “a field hospital”.
His link to Turkey
In November 2014 he visited Ankara and Istanbul and prayed together with Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew.
His death
He died on 21 April 2025, Easter Monday. The day before he had given the Easter blessing.
docs: The light of faith; an encyclical begun by Benedict XVI.
The joy of the Gospel (apostolic exhortation).
On care for our common home.
The love of the Sacred Heart of Jesus.

popes.name: Pope Leo XIV
popes.cat: Current Pontiff
popes.bio: Robert Francis Prevost was elected on 8 May 2025. He is the first pope from the United States and worked for many years as a missionary in Peru. He is an Augustinian friar.
secs: His life

He was born in Chicago in 1955. He joined the Order of St. Augustine, worked in Peru as a missionary and teacher, and later became prior general of his order. In 2015 he became bishop of Chiclayo in Peru, and in 2023 head of the Vatican office responsible for bishops.
The name Leo

He said he chose his name in memory of Leo XIII: just as Leo answered the industrial revolution, the Church today must answer the questions the age of artificial intelligence raises about human dignity and work.
His link to Turkey
In November 2025, for the 1700th anniversary of the Council of Nicaea, he came to Turkey and prayed together with Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew in İznik.
docs: An apostolic exhortation on love for the poor; a text begun by Pope Francis.
